case.case_title: Lerins Peiris v. Neil Rupasinghe, Member of Parliament and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, SC Application 126/99 (FR), decided on 19 November 1999

clause.text: Freedom of speech and expression including publication.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression guaranteed by Article 14(1)(a) was violated when he was expelled from a workshop and assaulted, preventing his participation.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that the respondents prevented him from exercising his right to free speech and expression by assaulting him and forcing him to leave the workshop, thereby violating Article 14(1)(a).
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that they were present as elected representatives and that the petitioner left voluntarily after being persuaded by the police and the venue manager; they denied responsibility for any violation.
key_facts: The petitioner was Chairman of a non-governmental organization involved in the Muturajawela Project.
The petitioner was invited to a workshop on 5 January 1999 but was told by respondents he should be kept out.
The petitioner was assaulted by respondents and forced to leave the meeting.
The petitioner made a police complaint and received medical treatment.
The respondents were acting in their official capacity as elected representatives.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court held that freedom of speech and expression is essential for democracy and must be protected even if the ideas expressed are controversial or offensive. The right includes the ability to participate in public discussions without fear of harassment or assault.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The respondents’ conduct in assaulting the petitioner and forcing him to leave the workshop was executive action chargeable to the State and effectively prevented the petitioner from exercising his right to free speech and expression under Article 14(1)(a).
principles_established: Freedom of speech includes the right to express controversial or unpopular ideas lawfully.
Elected representatives must uphold constitutional fundamental rights and cannot abridge them.
Executive action includes conduct by persons acting under color of office that restricts fundamental rights.
precedents_cited: Wijeratne v. Vijitha Perera and Others
Faiz v. Attorney General and Others
Deshapriya and Another v. Municipal Council, Nuwara Eliya and two others
Channa Pieris v. Attorney General and Others
Red Lion Broadcasting Co. v. F.C.C.
Federal Communications Commission v. League of Women Voters
National Association for the Advancement of Colored People v. Alabama Ex Rel. Patterson
West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette

outcome.holding: The court declared that the first to fifth respondents violated the petitioner’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression guaranteed by Article 14(1)(a).
outcome.remedy_or_orders: The respondents were ordered to pay the petitioner Rs. 50,000 each as compensation and Rs. 5,000 each as costs within three months.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 14(1)(a) was central to the court’s reasoning as the petitioner’s exclusion and assault directly infringed his constitutionally guaranteed freedom of speech and expression, which the court emphasized as vital to democracy.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioner was assaulted and forced to leave a workshop, preventing him from exercising his right to free speech and expression; the court held this conduct violated Article 14(1)(a).
